analysis.one_liner: Cuts federal pension and health benefits for ex-lawmakers and senior staff who become lobbyists.
analysis.headline: The bill, which would have stripped federal retirement and health benefits from former members of Congress and senior staff who become registered lobbyists, never received a hearing or a vote in the 118th Congress.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would bar a former member of Congress or a former senior congressional employee from collecting federal retirement benefits, health coverage, or life insurance for any month in which they work and are paid as a registered lobbyist. It covers pensions under both civil service retirement systems, the Thrift Savings Plan, federal health benefits including dental and vision, and federal group life insurance. Members and staff who have already earned the money in their own retirement accounts keep it; the rule applies to people who leave Congress after the bill becomes law. The bill was introduced in April 2023, referred to two House committees, and received no further action before the Congress ended in January 2025.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary taxpayers and voters. If it had passed, members of Congress and top aides could no longer cash in on the revolving door by lobbying after leaving office and still draw a federal pension and government health coverage, and the public would gain a modest check on the practice of legislators writing rules one year and lobbying on them the next.

how_it_helps.text: Prohibits a former member of Congress or former senior congressional employee who is a registered lobbyist and entitled to lobbyist compensation from receiving any federal retirement, health, or life insurance benefits for months they work as a lobbyist [S2][S3].

Covers the Civil Service Retirement System and Federal Employees' Retirement System (including the Thrift Savings Plan), the Federal Employees Health Benefits Program including enhanced dental and vision benefits, and the Federal Employees' Group Life Insurance Program [S2][S3].

Defines the rules broadly: 'senior congressional employee' includes legislative-branch staff at or above 120% of GS-15 pay for at least 60 days, one principal assistant designated by each member, and comparable GAO positions; 'registered lobbyist' includes agents registered under the Foreign Agents Registration Act [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Former members of Congress and senior congressional aides who would go on to work as registered lobbyists after leaving office. They would lose federal retirement and health benefits for any month they are paid as a lobbyist, creating a direct personal financial cost for taking the lobbying path.
analysis.who_pays_short: Ex-lawmakers and senior staff who lobby

drawbacks.text: The penalty is tied only to registered lobbying. A former member could lobby informally, or work for a lobbying firm in a role that does not trigger registration, and keep full federal benefits — so the incentive to pass through the revolving door may be narrowed but not eliminated [S3].
The restriction applies prospectively only, to people who become former members or senior employees after enactment, so anyone already in the pipeline keeps benefits [S3].

The benefit forfeiture is a blunt instrument: it penalizes the individual's personal earned retirement security rather than restricting the lobbying activity itself, and its deterrent effect on revolving-door lobbying is untested.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The policy is a reasonable, if modest, ethics measure: it imposes a real personal cost on the most visible revolving-door path while carefully protecting retirement money the individual already earned. Its main weakness is that it targets registered lobbying only, leaving easier workarounds. But the larger issue is that it never received any consideration — no hearing, no markup, no vote — so its merits were never weighed at all.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced and referred to the House Administration and Oversight and Accountability committees in April 2023, and neither committee ever took it up before the 118th Congress ended in January 2025.

narrative.text: Rep. Bill Posey (R-FL) introduced the bill on April 6, 2023 [S1][S2].

The same day, it was referred to the Committee on House Administration and, in addition, to the Committee on Oversight and Accountability, for consideration of provisions within each committee's jurisdiction [S5].
No committee hearing, markup, or floor action followed; the bill received no cosponsors and died at the end of the 118th Congress on January 3, 2025 [S4][S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Former members of Congress and senior congressional staff who go on to become registered lobbyists keep their full federal pensions and health benefits, because no committee ever acted on the bill.

for.name: Rep. Bill Posey
for.what_they_did: Introduced the End the Congressional Revolving Door Act on April 6, 2023

sides.party_line_note: The bill had a single Republican sponsor and no cosponsors from either party, so no meaningful partisan pattern can be read from the record [S4].

industries.industry: Registered lobbying firms and the lobbying industry
industries.note: The bill raises the personal cost to former members and senior staff of joining the registered lobbying workforce, shrinking the pool of high-influence talent available to lobbying employers. Because it targets only registered lobbying, it may push revolving-door activity toward unregistered influence work rather than ending it.

industries.industry: Federal employee retirement and benefits programs (OPM-administered)
industries.note: OPM and the Thrift Savings Plan would have to administer the new eligibility rule and write regulations. The administrative burden is modest, and the programs' interest in serving members is unaffected for everyone except ex-lawmakers-turned-lobbyists.
